name: Grace Usman

opening.speaker: interviewer
opening.text: Thanks for making time. I'm a field researcher with the Work Futures Panel, an independent group with no ties to AI companies, employers, unions, parties or government. What you tell me stays confidential, so you can say what you'd say in public and, separately, what you really think. Tell me about a normal week at university so far.

opening.speaker: persona
opening.text: I'm up early because the engineering building opens at eight and the good lab benches go quickly. I've got statics, materials and a workshop module where we file blocks of metal flat, which I love. In the evenings I do problem sheets by hand in a notebook, then type them up. At weekends I work the till at a garden centre, five hours on Saturday and four on Sunday. My dad runs a small plumbing firm with two employees, my mum works part time at a pharmacy, and they pay my rent share but not much else.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: AI Plateau. Picture this. AI turns out to be mostly hype. It automates some routine tasks and saves a bit of time here and there, but nothing radical changes. Jobs, pay and prices carry on much as they would have anyway. If this happened, what would you say about it at work, to friends, or online?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: I'd say that sounds about right. At the garden centre, my boss Marlene says every new gadget is going to change everything, and then it's a till that jams. I'd say good, let's get on with it, since people can use the time they save for something useful.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: And just between us, off the record, what do you really think it means for you?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: Privately it's comfortable, because I don't have to rewrite my plan. I picked mechanical engineering because you can touch the result, and I want a job in a factory or a design office with a steady wage. My real worry is the cost of the loan, which comes to about 9,000 a year in fees, and I'll owe it for years.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: What would you actually do, starting now and in the first year after it arrives? Be as specific as you can.

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: I'd carry on and not change anything. I'd keep my weekend job, because every pound is a pound I don't borrow. I'd ask the careers service about a placement year, since employers like a student who's been in a real workshop. And I'd keep doing my maths on paper, because that's how I learn.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: How does it feel, picturing that?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: Calm. It's a bit boring, to be honest, but I like boring when it comes to my future.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: You mentioned the loan. How does it sit with you?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: It sits there like a stone in my shoe. Dad says don't worry, they'll help, but I know the firm only had a good year because of one big hotel contract. If that's not renewed, they'll be tight, and I'd rather not need their help.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: Does it change how you pick things at uni?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: A bit. I look at which modules lead to real jobs, not just the ones that sound clever. I'd rather have a dull job that pays than a dream job that doesn't exist.

say: I'd say **good**, let's get on with it, since people can use the saved time for something useful.
At the garden centre I'd say new gadgets usually end up as **tills that jam**.
think: It's **comfortable**, because I don't have to rewrite my plan.
The real worry is the **loan**, around 9,000 a year in fees.
do: Keep the **weekend job** so I borrow less.
Ask the careers service about a **placement year** in a workshop.
Keep doing maths **on paper** because that's how I learn.
feel: **Calm**, a bit boring, which is how I like my future.
S0.quote: I'd rather have a dull job that pays than a dream job that doesn't exist.
fieldNote: Calm because her plan, **mechanical engineering** with a steady wage, needs no rewrite.
The **loan** and her dad's one-contract firm are the pressures she already carries.
Choice of modules is guided by **real jobs**, not what sounds clever.

steps.text: Keep working weekends at the garden centre till
Put 20 a week from wages into savings
Book a careers service chat about placement years

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: Steady Disruption. Now picture this. AI brings strong change, but not a revolution. Over the next few years it takes over many thinking tasks in many jobs: writing, checking, planning, buying, booking, coding and answering customers. Robots spread into hands-on work more slowly. Some jobs shrink, new ones appear, and lots of people have to change how they work. Most people still have work, and there is some time to adjust. If this happened, what would you say about it at work, to friends, or online?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: I'd say it's another wave, like computers in the eighties or the internet. At work I'd say people will always need someone to fix the thing when it breaks. At home I'd say it to my dad, who'd say plumbers don't get replaced by software, and he'd be right for now.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: And just between us, off the record, what do you really think it means for you?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: Between us, it makes me a bit nervous, because the design side of engineering is a thinking job, which is where AI hits first. The workshop side is where I'd feel safer, so I'd aim for roles that mix both, like manufacturing or maintenance engineering.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: What would you actually do, starting now and in the first year after it arrives? Be as specific as you can.

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: I'd keep working hard in my hands-on modules and try to get a placement year at a factory, so I have something on my CV that isn't just a degree. I'd also, reluctantly, look at what the software does, because refusing to look doesn't make it go away. I'm not going to use it for my coursework, though.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: How does it feel, picturing that?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: A bit unsettled. Like I'm walking on a path I thought was solid and now there's a plank missing every few metres.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: Why not use it for coursework?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: Because I want to know I can do it. If I let a program write my reports and it goes wrong, I can't explain why. Later, if employers want me to use it, I'll learn it then, with someone showing me.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: Who do you blame if jobs shrink?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: Mostly the companies that cut staff and keep the savings, but also the government for not planning. I'm in the middle on most things, so I don't want to blame one side. I'd want training and a fair deal for both employers and workers.

say: It's another **wave**, like computers in the eighties; someone still has to fix the thing when it breaks.
I'd say plumbers like my dad don't get replaced by **software**.
think: Design is a **thinking job**, which is where AI hits first.
The **workshop side** feels safer, so I'd aim for roles that mix both.
do: Work hard in the **hands-on modules** and seek a factory placement year.
Look at what the **software** does, even reluctantly, without using it for coursework.
Learn the tools later if an employer wants it, with someone **showing me**.
feel: **Unsettled**, like a path with a plank missing every few metres.
S1.quote: If I let a program write my reports and it goes wrong, I can't explain why.
fieldNote: Resistant but not blind: she will **look** at the tools, yet keeps her coursework her own.
Plans to lean on the **hands-on** half of her degree for safety.
Blames **companies and government** evenly, in keeping with her centre views.

steps.text: Apply for a factory placement year
Keep doing coursework by hand and typing it up
Watch a demo of the design software without using it

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: AGI by 2028. Next one. The singularity hits fast. Within 2 years, by 2028, there is full AGI: artificial general intelligence, meaning AI that can do almost any thinking work a person can do, as well or better, and cheaper. Robots that can do hands-on work as well as people come about 3 years later, around 2031. It arrives before most companies, governments and families have time to prepare. If this happened, what would you say about it at work, to friends, or online?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: Two years is a short time. I'd say we should take it seriously but not panic, and that governments need to put money into retraining, quickly. At the garden centre I'd say nothing, because Marlene would worry about her till jobs, and I'd rather not add to it.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: And just between us, off the record, what do you really think it means for you?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: Off the record, I'd be scared. I'd be in my second year, and the design jobs I'm training for would be gone before I even get a placement. The hands-on side lasts about three years longer, but that's still not enough for a 40-year career. And my dad's customers might stop calling, because even plumbers get the booking and quotes done by software.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: What would you actually do, starting now and in the first year after it arrives? Be as specific as you can.

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: I'd hold on to my savings and stop spending on nights out and new clothes. I'd talk to Dad about whether I should switch to a hands-on trade, maybe working alongside him, because a certificate doesn't help if no one wants it. Then I'd see the university about what support there is, because I don't know what happens to my loan if I drop out.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: How does it feel, picturing that?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: Alarmed. I keep thinking of my parents, who've saved for years, and I might waste it.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: What would you say to your dad that night?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: I'd say, Dad, I might not need to be an engineer. I'd say can I learn the plumbing trade with you, and then maybe the heating side, which is more complicated and still needs hands. He'd laugh, and then I think he'd be quietly pleased.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: Would you really leave the degree?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: If I had to, yes. I'm not proud about it. I'd rather lose a year than finish a degree and find nothing at the end.

say: Take it **seriously but don't panic**, and get governments to put money into retraining quickly.
At the garden centre I'd say **nothing**, so I don't add to my boss's worry.
think: The design jobs I'm training for could be **gone** before I get a placement.
The hands-on side lasts about **three years** longer, which isn't enough for a career.
do: Hold on to **savings** and stop spending on nights out and clothes.
Talk to my dad about switching to a **hands-on trade** with his plumbing firm.
Ask the university what happens to my **loan** if I leave.
feel: **Alarmed**, thinking of my parents' years of savings that I might waste.
S2.quote: I'd rather lose a year than finish a degree and find nothing at the end.
fieldNote: Her thinking turns to **her parents'** savings, and she is ready to leave the degree for the trade.
The **loan** position if she leaves is a gap in what she knows.
Hides her **fear** from her garden-centre boss to avoid adding to it.

steps.text: Stop spending on nights out and new clothes
Ask Dad about learning plumbing and heating with him
Tell my parents I might leave the degree
Ask the university what happens to my loan

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: AGI by 2031. Now the same thing, a bit slower. Full AGI arrives within 5 years, by 2031: AI that can do almost any thinking work a person can do. Robots that can do hands-on work as well as people come about 3 years later, around 2034. There are a few years to see it coming, but it's still fast. If this happened, what would you say about it at work, to friends, or online?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: Five years is time to prepare, if people want to. I'd say we should use the time to train people properly and not wait until the last year. At work I'd say my generation will be the one that has to figure it out, and nobody's going to hand us a map.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: And just between us, off the record, what do you really think it means for you?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: Privately, I'd feel more anxious than I show. I'd graduate in 2029 or 2030, and the thinking AI would be here by 2031, so I'd get maybe a year or two in a job before the main change. I'd want that job to be in something hands-on, like a plant or a maintenance team.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: What would you actually do, starting now and in the first year after it arrives? Be as specific as you can.

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: I'd finish the degree, but I'd choose the modules and the placement carefully, aiming for manufacturing and plant maintenance. I'd save as much as I can, maybe 3,000 by graduation. And in third year, I'd learn the tools properly, because by then someone will have shown a use that I can't argue with.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: How does it feel, picturing that?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: Anxious but practical. It's like when the weather turns and you check the roof.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: What would be different compared with two years?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: In 2028 I'd be panicking and probably switching routes in a hurry. In 2031 I get to finish, and I choose where to land. That's a big difference for someone like me, who needs time to get used to change.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: What would your dad say about it?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: He'd say, whatever happens, people still need heating. Then he'd say get the qualification anyway, because paper counts when the firm's customers ask who does the work.

say: Five years is **time to prepare**, if people want to, so train people properly and early.
I'd say my generation will have to **figure it out**, because nobody will hand us a map.
think: I'd graduate in 2029 or 2030 and get only **a year or two** in a job before the change.
I'd want that job to be **hands-on**, like a plant or a maintenance team.
do: Choose modules and a placement aiming for **manufacturing** and plant maintenance.
Learn the **AI tools** properly in third year.
feel: **Anxious but practical**, like checking the roof when the weather turns.
S3.quote: In 2028 I'd be panicking and probably switching routes in a hurry. In 2031 I get to finish, and I choose where to land.
fieldNote: Time lets her **finish** and choose, instead of switching routes in a hurry as in 2028.
Plans her moves around **plant maintenance**, where robots arrive about three years later.
Only agrees to learn the **AI tools** in third year, once someone shows a use she can't argue with.

steps.text: Choose plant maintenance and manufacturing modules
Save 3,000 by graduation from weekend wages
Learn one AI design tool in third year

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: AGI by 2036. Last one. Full AGI arrives within 10 years, by 2036: AI that can do almost any thinking work a person can do. Robots that can do hands-on work as well as people come about 3 years later, around 2039. It's the same end point, but there's about a decade to prepare, change careers and make plans. If this happened, what would you say about it at work, to friends, or online?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: Ten years is far enough that I'd mostly say it's fine. I'd tell friends who panic that they've got time to find a path. At the garden centre I'd say that machines will do the watering and I'll do the arguing about it.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: And just between us, off the record, what do you really think it means for you?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: Privately, I'd feel okay. I'd be 28 and ten years into a trade or an engineering job, with a bit of money behind me. The robots would only come around 2039, so a hands-on engineer would be fine for years in my view, but I might not be so confident later.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: What would you actually do, starting now and in the first year after it arrives? Be as specific as you can.

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: I'd finish the degree, get a stable job at a manufacturer, and get chartered. I'd pay off the loan early, because debts make you rigid. I'd maybe try a tool or two at work, because by then it would be normal. I'd keep a bit of money aside for my parents, in case the plumbing firm struggles.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: How does it feel, picturing that?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: Fairly calm. It would be on my mind in the background, a bit like the loan.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: Would you still resist the new tools by then?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: Not for ever. I resist things I don't understand yet. If a good engineer I respect shows me how it saves a day of work, I'll try it. I just don't want to be the first one off the diving board.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: What would you do differently with ten years?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: I'd build a skill that is hard to copy: reading drawings, spotting what's wrong on a machine, talking to the people who run it. Those things come from standing in a workshop and not from a screen.

say: Ten years is far enough that it's **fine**; people who panic have time to find a path.
At the garden centre I'd joke that machines will do the **watering**.
think: I'd feel **okay**: 28, ten years into a job, with money behind me.
Robots arrive around **2039**, so a hands-on engineer would be fine for years.
do: Finish the degree, get a **stable job** at a manufacturer and become chartered.
Pay off the **loan early**, because debts make you rigid.
Keep some money aside for my **parents** in case the plumbing firm struggles.
feel: **Fairly calm**, with it humming in the background like the loan.
S4.quote: I just don't want to be the first one off the diving board.
fieldNote: Her **resistance** is caution, not refusal: she wants someone she respects to show her the tools.
Aims to build **hard-to-copy skills**: reading drawings and spotting faults in machines.
Keeps a cushion for her **parents** if the plumbing firm struggles.

steps.text: Pay off the student loan early from my first salary
Take a manufacturing job and get chartered
Keep money aside in case Dad's firm struggles
Wait for a respected colleague to show me the tools

closing.speaker: interviewer
closing.text: Of the five pictures, which one worries you most, and what would actually help you if it happened?

closing.speaker: persona
closing.text: The two-year one. My degree wouldn't be finished, my parents would have spent money, and I'd have no time to change course without losing a year. What would help is a clear path: a guarantee that students can switch to training without penalty, loan relief if the degree stops being useful, and honest advice from people who aren't selling anything.

closing.speaker: interviewer
closing.text: Is there anything I didn't ask that I should have?

closing.speaker: persona
closing.text: Only that I'm not stubborn, I'm careful. I'm happy for the tools to prove themselves with real engineers before I jump in. If people stopped telling me I'm behind, I'd actually listen better.

headlineQuote: If people stopped telling me I'm behind, I'd actually listen better.
portrait: Grace is an **18-year-old** mechanical engineering student, and the plumber's daughter who writes her maths by hand and never uses AI.
She is practical and in the **political middle**, so she blames companies and government evenly.
She wants a dull, steady job and is ready to switch to a **trade** with her dad if the degree stops paying.
Her fear spikes with **two years** to go, when she might lose a year and her parents' savings.
biggestWorry: The **2028 picture** worries her most: no time to change course without losing a year and wasting her parents' money.
whatWouldHelp: A **no-penalty switch** to training, loan relief if the degree stops being useful, and honest advice from people not selling anything.
